questions.question: What are JavaScript ES modules, and how are they loaded and evaluated?
questions.title: ES Module Loading and Evaluation
questions.direct_answer: An ES module is a file with its own scope that declares dependencies and public bindings through `import` and `export`. Static imports form a dependency graph before evaluation; modules run in strict mode, execute once per resolved module identity, and are deferred by default when loaded in browsers with `type="module"`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand module scope, dependency linking, one-time evaluation, and browser loading requirements.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Running browser modules from `file://`, omitting `type="module"`, or expecting imported names to become global.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Separate resolution, linking, and evaluation, then explain why repeated imports share one module instance.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Each ES module has its own scope; declarations do not automatically become global variables.
Static `import` declarations are top-level and let the runtime build the dependency graph before execution.
Module code runs in strict mode automatically.
A resolved module is evaluated once, then its module instance is reused by importers.
Browsers load module scripts with `type="module"` and apply URL and CORS rules.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
An ES module is a JavaScript file with its own scope and an explicit public interface. `export` makes selected bindings available, while `import` declares which bindings another module needs. Other declarations remain inside the module instead of becoming properties on the global object. Module code also runs in strict mode automatically.

Static import declarations let the runtime prepare a dependency graph before normal statements run. It resolves each module specifier, links imported names to real exported bindings, prepares dependencies, and then evaluates module bodies. This early linking is why a missing named export can be reported before application logic reaches the importing statement.

A module is normally evaluated once for one resolved module identity. Several importers of the same URL share its namespace and top-level state instead of rerunning initialization for each importer. This avoids repeating the same setup for every consumer. The example imports one data-URL module twice: both imports return the same namespace object, and the top-level counter increases only once.

A browser entry script uses `type="module"`; module scripts are deferred by default, and their specifiers are resolved as URLs under CORS rules. Serving modules over HTTP avoids common `file://` restrictions. Static imports suit required dependencies. Dynamic `import(specifier)` is an expression that returns a Promise and suits conditional or lazy loading, while using the same module identity rules.

sections.title: Concept: ES Module Loading and Evaluation
sections.content:
**Three phases.** Resolution finds module identifiers, linking connects imported names to exported bindings, and evaluation runs module bodies after their dependencies are prepared. This is why static syntax can be checked before normal statements execute.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  E[Entry module] --> R[Resolve dependency specifiers]
  R --> L[Link imports to exports]
  L --> D[Evaluate dependencies]
  D --> V[Evaluate entry once]
  V --> N[Reuse module namespace]
```

**Runnable example.** Two imports of the same data-URL module share one evaluation and one namespace object.

```javascript
const source = "globalThis.moduleRuns = (globalThis.moduleRuns || 0) + 1; export const value = 7;";
const url = "data:text/javascript," + encodeURIComponent(source);
const first = await import(url);
const second = await import(url);

console.log(first.value);          // 7
console.log(first === second);     // true
console.log(globalThis.moduleRuns); // 1
```

**Boundary.** Module identity is based on the resolved specifier. Different URLs, including meaningful query strings, may create distinct module instances even when they return the same source text.

questions.question: What is the difference between named exports, default exports, namespace imports, and import aliases?
questions.title: Named and Default Module Exports
questions.direct_answer: Named exports expose bindings under explicit exported names and are imported with braces; a module can have many. A module can have at most one default export, imported without braces under a local name chosen by the importer. Namespace imports collect exported names in a module namespace object, while `as` resolves local name conflicts.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can write and explain each import form without confusing source export names and local bindings.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Adding braces around a default import or omitting braces from a named import.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that default is a special export name and aliases only change the importing module's local name.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Named import syntax uses braces and must match an exported name unless `as` renames it.
A module may export many named bindings but only one `default` binding.
A default import uses no braces and its local name is chosen by the importing module.
`import * as tools` creates a module namespace object accessed as `tools.name`.
Import forms do not copy ordinary values; they connect to module exports according to module binding rules.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Named exports give public bindings explicit exported names, and one module may have many of them. `export const version = 2` is imported with braces as `import { version } from "./tools.js"`. The imported name stays connected to that export; the braces select a name and do not create an object destructuring copy.

A module may have at most one default export because `default` is a special export name. It is imported without braces, as in `import parse from "./tools.js"`. The importing file chooses the local name, so another file may call the same default export `read`; that choice does not rename anything in the source module.

`import * as tools from "./tools.js"` creates a module namespace object whose properties expose the module's exports, such as `tools.double`. It is useful when several names form a clear group. The namespace is not an ordinary mutable record, so assigning to an exported property is not an alternative way to change module state.

An alias changes only the consumer's local label: `import { version as apiVersion }` still reads the source export named `version`. Default and named exports can coexist, and another import may use the namespace form. The two-file example places each syntax beside the declaration it refers to, making the source name and local name visible.

sections.title: Concept: Named and Default Module Exports
sections.content:
**Binding map.** Export names belong to the source module. Local import names belong to the consumer. Named syntax keeps those names aligned by default; aliases and default imports deliberately separate them.

| Source export | Import form | Local access |
|---|---|---|
| `export const version = 1` | `import { version }` | `version` |
| same named export | `import { version as apiVersion }` | `apiVersion` |
| `export default parse` | `import read` | `read` |
| all exports | `import * as parser` | `parser.version` |

**Runnable example.** Dynamic import returns the same namespace shape, which lets one self-contained program demonstrate default and named access.

```javascript
const source = [
  "export const version = 2;",
  "export function double(value) { return value * 2; }",
  "export default function parse(value) { return Number(value); }",
].join("\n");
const moduleUrl = "data:text/javascript," + encodeURIComponent(source);
const tools = await import(moduleUrl);

console.log(tools.default("4")); // 4
console.log(tools.double(4));      // 8
console.log(tools.version);        // 2
```

**Boundary.** Re-export barrels can simplify imports but may hide dependency direction or create cycles. A small feature module often reads more clearly when consumers import from the file that owns the symbol.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  E[Source module exports] -->|named binding| N[import with braces]
  E -->|default binding| D[import without braces]
  E -->|all exported bindings| S[namespace object]
  N -->|as| A[local alias]
```

questions.question: What are live bindings in ES modules, and how do they affect imports, cycles, and dynamic loading?
questions.title: ES Module Live Bindings
questions.direct_answer: An ES module import is a read-only local view of the exporter's binding, not a one-time copied value. When the exporting module updates a mutable exported binding, importers observe the new value; importers cannot assign to that imported name. Cycles can work through linking but fail when code reads a binding before initialization.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand imported binding identity, update ownership, cycle initialization, and dynamic import.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling imports constant snapshots or trying to assign through an imported name or namespace property.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use a binding-cell mental model and connect unsafe cycles to reads before initialization rather than saying all cycles fail.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Imported names are live views of exported bindings rather than snapshots.
The exporting module may update an exported `let`, and importers see the update.
An importer cannot assign directly to an imported binding.
Cyclic modules are linked, but early reads of uninitialized bindings can throw `ReferenceError`.
Dynamic `import(specifier)` returns a Promise for the module namespace and supports conditional loading.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
An ES module import is a live, read-only view of a binding owned by the exporting module; it is not a value copied once at import time. If the exporter changes an exported `let`, a later read in every importer sees the new value. Importers receive current access to that binding, not ownership of it.

The importing module cannot assign to the imported name or use a namespace property to overwrite it. The exporter may expose a function that performs an allowed update. In the example, `increment()` changes the exporter's `count`, and the imported namespace reports `1` on the next read without being imported again.

Live bindings allow cyclic module graphs to be linked, so a cycle is not automatically an error. The danger is evaluation timing. If module A reads module B's lexical export before B has initialized it, the read can throw `ReferenceError`. Delaying the read may work, but removing the cycle usually produces clearer ownership and initialization order.

Static imports declare required dependencies at module top level so tools and the runtime can analyze them early. `import(specifier)` runs as an expression and returns a Promise for a module namespace, which fits optional or lazy features. For the same resolved identity it reuses the module instance and exposes the same live bindings rather than creating a fresh copy each time.

sections.title: Concept: ES Module Live Bindings
sections.content:
**Reference relationship.** The importer receives access to a binding cell, not permission to overwrite it. Reading consults the current cell value; updates happen only in the source module's environment.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  E[Exporter binding count] --> I1[Importer A reads current value]
  E --> I2[Importer B reads current value]
  U[Exporter increment function] --> E
  I1 -. assignment forbidden .-> E
```

**Runnable example.** The imported namespace reports the changed value after the exporting function updates its own binding.

```javascript
const source = [
  "export let count = 0;",
  "export function increment() { count += 1; }",
].join("\n");
const url = "data:text/javascript," + encodeURIComponent(source);
const counter = await import(url);

console.log(counter.count); // 0
counter.increment();
console.log(counter.count); // 1: live value
```

**Boundary.** A namespace object is not a normal mutable record. Its exported properties describe module bindings and cannot be reassigned as an alternative way to update exporter state.
